name: AI Documentation Tools at Trial Sites
blurb: Reducing the documentation load on site staff.
title: AI Documentation Tools at Trial Sites
answer: Much trial work at sites is documentation, and AI scribes and assistants built for clinical care are being applied to it. One vendor reported that at a large health system its AI documentation assistant cut time spent on clinical notes by 72 percent, the kind of saving trial sites are now seeking.

reading.body:
AI documentation tools are being applied to trial site paperwork on the strength of a 72 percent reduction in clinical note-writing time reported at one health system.

The pattern is a transfer of a tool built for one setting into another. Suki's assistant was measured at Rush University Medical Center on clinical notes, not on trial documentation. Trial sites are seeking that kind of saving because their documentation load duplicates work already done for patient care, and the staff carrying it are stretched.

The constraint is not the drafting. An AI generated source document still needs investigator review before it becomes trial data, and recording participants requires consent and adherence to the trial's approved procedures. The tool changes who writes the first draft, not who is accountable for the record.

What the data does not cover is whether the 72 percent figure holds at trial sites, where forms, adverse event reports, and sponsor correspondence differ from clinical notes. It reports one vendor's result at one institution, and no trial-site measurement.

explainer:
Trial sites carry a heavy documentation load: source records of each visit, case report form entries, adverse event reports, and correspondence with sponsors and ethics committees. Much of it duplicates clinical documentation already written for patient care, and it takes time from staff who are often stretched.

AI documentation assistants, first built for clinicians, draft notes from recorded conversations and pull information into structured forms. Applied carefully at trial sites, they can cut time spent on paperwork. Two rules apply. The investigator remains responsible for the accuracy of source documents, so every AI generated record must be reviewed and confirmed. And recording participants requires their consent and must follow the trial's approved procedures and privacy rules.

What documentation burden looks like at a site

A research coordinator at a trial site spends much of the day transcribing: recording visits in source documents, entering the same data into the sponsor's electronic data capture system, answering queries about discrepancies, and keeping the regulatory binder current. The same AI documentation tools that hospitals use for clinical notes, ambient recording that drafts a note from a conversation, are now being tried for trial visits, along with tools that pre fill data capture forms from the medical record.

Why it is harder than ordinary clinical use

Trial documentation is source data for a regulatory decision, and it is inspected. Three questions follow. Is the AI drafted note the source, or is the recording, and how long must each be kept? Does the drafting tool meet the sponsor's and the regulator's expectations for electronic records, including audit trails and controlled access? And has the patient consented to recording for research purposes, which is a different consent from recording for care? Sites and sponsors have to answer these before a tool touches a trial visit.

What is being learned

Early reports from sites point to real time savings on visit notes and data entry, and to fewer transcription discrepancies, which means fewer queries. They also point to the need for a coordinator to review every draft, because the tools miss trial specific details such as protocol deviations and dosing times that ordinary clinical notes do not emphasise. The sponsors that adopt fastest are those that validate the tool once and offer it to all their sites, rather than leaving each site to assess it alone.
